blocks.p: Okada Shizuka asked him back to the same small white room three days into Obon. This time there was no laminated card on the table. There was only a single thermal printout, curling at its edges the way thermal paper curls when a warm hand has held it too long. She did not slide it across to him. She laid her palm flat on top of it, as if the words might leave through the ceiling if she let go.
"The cycle ran Thursday," she said.

Rei felt the day land like a dropped stone. He remembered what she had made him promise, without quite letting him promise it. Do not let them assess him on a Thursday. He understood now that the warning had never been only about Gin.
"You weren't on the schedule," Okada said. "Sena flagged you anyway. The instrument reaches for whoever's nearest when a reading goes deep, and you were in the building."

She turned the sheet over. The anomaly was not a number. It was a shape. The assessment array drew a medium's registers as a pair of nested rings. A citizen came out as clean concentric circles. A fever-case came out as a fat smeared lozenge. Rei's were neither. His were two rings that should have been quiet and were instead leaning, both of them, toward a third mark that did not belong to him. It was a faint bright knot off to the north of the page, like a moon that had wandered into the wrong sky.

"The textbook word for this is domain incipient," she said, very evenly, the way a doctor gives a diagnosis she has decided not to be frightened of yet. "It means the machine thinks something is being built inside you. Or that something has already keyed in, and is reading you the way you read everyone else."

Obon hummed through the building's tired air conditioning. Paper lanterns sagged over the intake desk for the dead who were meant to come home gently this week. Rei thought of the third mark, and how it leaned north. Toward Kita. Toward a wall someone was patiently thinning.
Okada watched his hands, the way she had the first day.

"I have eleven hours before the cycle closes and the reading becomes a record," she said. "Once it's a record it goes up. To the Auditors. To the families above Adachi. To anyone who can act on a domain forming inside a registered medium. And what they do to a domain that's forming is close it. Early. While it's small enough to close."
She lifted her palm off the page at last.
"So. Before it's a record, it's still just a thing two people in a white room are looking at. What do you want it to be?"

blocks.cap: The Internal Affairs and Audit floor

blocks.p: The way down to the array ran through Internal Affairs and Audit. Okada badged them through a door with no sign on it, and the noise of the building dropped away.

It looked like the dullest room in the Directorate. Cabinets. Terminals. Very little talking. A plant on a windowsill that someone remembered to water. At the far desk a man in his thirties sat reading a file with his tea going cold beside him. He did not look up when they passed. Rei had the uncomfortable sense that he had been seen anyway, completely, by someone who was watching the whole room instead of the people in it.

blocks.cap: Moriya Tatsuki, sixteen years in Internal Affairs

blocks.p: "Moriya," Okada said quietly, when they were past. "Sixteen years in Internal Affairs. He runs this floor. He's one of the good ones." She paused. "Gin used to say that's exactly why the floor frightened him. A good man with the power to file is still a man with the power to file."
Next to Moriya's office was a second desk, bare. No photographs. No papers. Only a fountain pen, laid square to the edge of the blotter, old and expensive and very carefully placed.

"That's Sena's," Okada said. "Her father's pen. She doesn't use it anymore. Someone keeps it straight for her." She did not stop walking. "She has the Tower seat on this floor. The Auditor's chair that belongs, by an arrangement nobody wrote down, to a family."
"Which family?"

"Fujiwara-Kage." Okada said it the way people in the building said all seven of those names, Tsukishiro, Fujiwara-Kage, Orimoto, Higashiyama, Kuroda, Akiyama, Nishimura. Politely, and a little lower. "They're an investigation house. Edo. Their founders worked alongside the shogunate's intelligence men, and they've been reading people for the state ever since. Clairsentience runs in them like a family nose. They turn out Arbiters the way other families turn out lawyers."
They waited for the inner lift. Okada kept her voice down.

"Of all the Tower families, they're the one most deeply inside this building. Two of them work here in senior posts. One in the Research Division. One in the Auditor network. Whether that's cooperation or infiltration depends on whose interest is being served that week. Probably both." Her mouth tightened. "The Grid says the family has been quietly documenting the Directorate's classified work for forty years. I've never been able to prove it. I've never tried very hard."
"And the Directorate lets them."

"The Directorate needs them. Gin will have written the whole arrangement down somewhere. The short version. They give it rank and training and cover, and it looks the other way, and a Tower child who joins us rises faster than their number earns." The lift came. "When I say the families above Adachi, that's who I mean."

doc.title: From Gin's book. Chapter Sixteen. On the Fujiwara-Kage.
lines: The Auditor network member from the Fujiwara-Kage, I know who it is and I am not naming them here.
My bi-monthly assessments are conducted by a different assessor than the one assigned to my district on the rotation schedule. I noticed this approximately two years ago. I have not raised it.
It may mean nothing. It may mean something that benefits me. It may mean something that does not. I continue to pass the assessments and I continue to note the irregularity.

blocks.p: The assessment array lived two floors further down, behind a door marked with nothing but a cycle number. The room was colder than the rest of the Directorate on purpose. It was the cold of a place built to keep something still.

Rei had expected a machine. Clearance levels, boxes that go ping. There was a machine. It was a low ring of grey instrument set into the floor like a drain. But the thing the machine read through was a person. A young woman sat at the centre of the ring with her hands open on her knees and her eyes tracking nothing.
Okada said her name the way a person names a place they are sorry about.
"Sena. Fujiwara-Kage Sena. She was a reader. A good one. Arbiter grade, two clean registers, the kind the Directorate doesn't get to keep as a witness. So they didn't keep her as one."

Rei understood it before Okada finished, because he saw it the way he saw everything. What he saw in Sena was a held breath where a person should be. They had hollowed her, gently. They had emptied the two registers until nothing of her own was left to colour a reading. So anyone the array pointed her at came back true, uncoloured, measured against a surface with no opinion of its own. She was the most honest instrument in Tokyo because there was nothing left of her to lie.

"She consented," Okada said, and the sentence cost her something to carry across the cold room. "Eight years ago. Terms in her own hand. She thought it was service. Her family thought it was a seat. The form doesn't have a box for what it actually is."
Sena's eyes found him then, slowly. For one moment something moved behind them that was almost recognition. It was the way a still pond moves when a fish turns, far below the surface.
"Gin's off-rotation assessor," Rei said. "For two years. It was her."

Okada did not answer, which was an answer. She took a laminated sheet from a pocket by the door and handed it to him. It was the protocol every registered medium sat through every two months, the one they were told was routine.

doc.title: Bi-Monthly Assessment Protocol. What Is Checked
lines: Stability profile. Current floor and ceiling against the registered baseline. Flagged if the floor has dropped more than fifteen percent from baseline, or the gap between floor and ceiling has narrowed. The most common flag.
Ability profile consistency. Verifies the registered type is still accurate. The instruments read against the standard single-path taxonomy. Capability outside it reads as instrument noise.
Register bleed. Emotional material picked up from heavy entity work. A grief-heavy caseload leaves grief in the signature.
Possession and cohabitation check. Assessors read for the double-layer signature of possession or cohabitation. Not disclosed to practitioners.
Behavioral review. Case history, supervisor report, flagged incidents. The most subjective part.

blocks.p: Under the fourth line, someone had written in pencil, in a hand Rei knew. The check catches entities that do not know what to hide. It does not catch entities that do.

"He passed every one," Okada said. "Clean. Before the fourteenth and after it. A thing that has studied a man for long enough knows what the assessment is measuring. It sits in the chair and gives the instrument what the instrument expects. A clean file doesn't mean he's uncompromised. It means whatever's in him is either absent or good enough at this. The file can't tell you which."

When the array woke, it did not ping. It tightened. The cold in the room drew inward toward the ring. Rei felt his own two registers, pressed flat his whole life, come half awake against his will. They reached toward the empty surface at the centre of the room the way water finds the lowest place.
This was the reading that had flagged him, run live. On the array's grey panel the rings bloomed again. His two, leaning. And the third bright knot to the north.

Now that he was inside the reading, he could feel the truth the page could only diagram. The knot was not in him. It was reaching for him, from a long way off, from a direction he knew. It was patient and fond and it wore a familiarity he would have recognised anywhere, because it was his brother's. It wore it like a borrowed coat, and it was not him.
Okada showed him the thing she was always going to have to show him. He could not decide what the reading became until he knew it could become anything.

The array kept a calibration log, a record of every adjustment ever made to true the instrument. She scrolled it back past his Thursday, past months, to a column of small corrections that were not corrections at all.

"The families above Adachi don't delete readings," she said. "Deleting leaves a hole, and holes get noticed. They recalibrate. They tell the instrument the honest answer is the error and feed it a kinder one, until the kinder one is what the machine believes."

Rei looked at the column and understood. The most honest instrument in Tokyo had been taught to lie so many times that its lies were now a fluent second language. This was how a possession became a clerical footnote. This was how a brother became a case closed too fast.
Rei stared at the column. "You could do that to mine," he said. It was not a question.

"I could. Tonight." Okada did not look away from the screen. "By morning the machine would believe you're a fever-case with a bad week. No Auditor would ever come down those stairs looking for you." She let that sit. "And the one reading anyone has ever taken that shows what's wearing your brother would be gone. I'd have done it with my own hands. You'd have stood here and watched me learn how."
"Then leave the reading. Give it a different cause." He heard himself reaching for it. "Festival bleed. Contamination from a witness. Something boring."

"Then it's bent." She said it gently, the way she might have told him a bone was broken. "A reading you bend once never lies straight again. You'd never trust it after. Not even the part of it that points at Gin."
"And if nobody touches it at all?"
Okada was quiet for a moment. The array ticked in the cold.

"Then it goes up. Up means the Auditors. What the Auditors do to a forming domain is close it early. Close you. Close whatever's reaching through you." Her voice stayed level, but her hand had found the edge of the panel and was holding it. "And they will not be gentle about which of you they decide is the patient."
Behind her, in the ring, Sena's open hands had not moved. But her head had turned a few degrees, toward the north, toward the same wrong moon.
Rei looked at the column of kind lies for a long moment. He thought of Gin passing every assessment, clean, while something sat in him and smiled at the instrument.
"Let it stand," he said. "It's the only true thing anyone in this building has written about him. I'm not going to be the next person who corrects it."
Okada closed her eyes briefly. Then she nodded and did not touch the log.

They came out of the reading room into a corridor where the Obon lanterns had begun to come down. The festival was closing. The dead were being seen back out, and the building was quietly resuming the business of pretending it never crossed to them at all. Whatever the array now believed about him would walk out in his file ahead of him, into rooms he would never see.
Okada walked him to the main lift and did not press the button. On the panel beside the doors one floor had no number, only a key slot. Rei looked at it.

blocks.cap: Containment and Reintegration, where a closed domain goes

blocks.p: "Containment and Reintegration," she said, following his eyes. "That's where a closed domain goes. The cells. They call it rehabilitation, and they say it gently. The staff are kind. They bring the contained tea and learn their names and mean the word care. And they still close the door. Entry is by order, not request." She was quiet for a second. "Gin walked that corridor once. He told me he counted the doors he didn't open, and he still hadn't decided if that was cowardice or mercy."
"Is there anywhere in this building that sees everything?" Rei asked. "Besides her."

"One room. I've never been in it. I've only had it described." Okada kept her eyes on the shut doors. "The Mirror Room. Surveillance. A long dark room with mirrors hung in rows to the ceiling, each one showing a slice of the city from a height no person stands at. The operators don't talk. They drink tea and watch through birds' eyes and write down what the city is feeling. They're on no roster I've ever seen. It never closes. Two people I trust have stood in it, and neither wanted to talk about it for long." She breathed out. "Between that room and this one, the building watches the whole city. It just doesn't always know what it's looking at."
Then she said what she had brought him to the lift to say.

"Gin knew this would happen. Not the details. The shape. A Thursday. An instrument. You in the building. A reading that points the wrong machine at the right truth. He spent his last free act trying to keep you off this page. And you've spent the morning deciding to be on it your own way."
The lift came. Neither of them stepped in.

There was one more thing the morning had handed him, and it was heavier than the reading. Sena had turned north. Twice he had watched the emptiest person in Tokyo lean toward Kita the way his own registers leaned. A hollowed instrument has no homesickness of its own to explain that. So the thing reaching for him through the array had been reaching for her too. It was testing every open surface in the building, patient and fond, wearing his brother's grain like a coat.

The knot was not waiting for assessment day. It was using it. Every cycle the Directorate ran was a door it propped open. The one institution able to close the wall in Kita had been holding a smaller door wide for years without ever knowing it.

"I can put one thing in the record before it locks," Okada said, quiet, the lift humming behind its shut doors. "A flag of my own. I can mark the array compromised. Pull Sena from the cycle. Blind the Directorate's truest eye, and give your brother's reaching nowhere to land for a while. Or I leave her in. I leave the door propped, and we keep the one instrument that ever told us the truth, knowing exactly what's using it to find you."
She looked at him the way she had over the laminated card on the first day, watching his hands more than his face.
"You've already decided what the page says. This decides whether the building keeps its eyes open, or shuts them to keep us safe. I won't make this one alone."

Rei thought of Sena's head turning, a few degrees at a time, toward the same place his own registers leaned. If they pulled her, the thing would go quiet in this building and they would lose the only window that showed it moving.
"Leave her in," he said. "If it's using her to look at me, then she's the one place we can watch it looking. Keep the eye open. I'll be careful what I let it see."
Okada held his gaze a moment longer. Then she reached past him and pressed the button, and the doors that had been open all this time finally began to close.
The lift rose through the building in silence. Somewhere around the third floor Rei's phone buzzed in his pocket.
He knew before he looked. The name at the top of the screen was his brother's.
You looked tired today, Rei. Go home and sleep. Please.

He had not told anyone where he was going this morning. He had not been anywhere today that a person could see him from, except a cold room two floors under the street, with a ring in the floor and a hollowed girl at its centre, turning her head toward the north.
